text:
"A young girl with SCID becomes an advocate for herself and others"

A must read story for all.

Seersha Sulack’s story is an inspiration for families affected by ‘bubble baby disease.’

By Nicole Chien | Jun 23, 2025 Patient Stories
This article was originally published by UCLA Health
Seersha Sulack’s childhood has been anything but ordinary.

For the first five years of her life, hospital rooms replaced playgrounds. Doctor visits took the place of playdates. Weekly injections became all too familiar. And avoiding exposure to germs always took priority.

Just days after birth, Seersha was diagnosed with ADA-SCID (adenosine deaminase-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency) — a rare genetic condition, also known as “bubble baby disease,” that impairs the immune systems of children.

Despite the constraints of her early life, Seersha remained driven by resilience and ambition. Now, at just 7 years old, she is a fearless self-advocate.

“Seersha is a firecracker. She speaks her mind and is really sweet,” says Donald Kohn, MD, a member of the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research at UCLA.

“Her energy is always up,” her mother, Shayla Sulack, adds. “She’s never met a stranger that she didn’t become friends with.”

That energy lit up Dodger Stadium on May 17, when Seersha was surprised with the opportunity to throw out the ceremonial first pitch and meet her favorite baseball player, Mookie Betts.

As she approached the pitcher’s mound and danced with excitement, Seersha was fulfilling a dream many would have thought impossible after her diagnosis.

Blood sample tells the story
Seersha was born Oct. 21, 2017, in a military hospital in Honolulu, Hawaii, the third child of the Sulack family.

The family’s jubilation quickly dimmed, however, when a routine blood test — including a standard SCID screening administered for all newborns in the U.S. — raised concern. A geneticist at the hospital discovered Seersha lacked T cells, a primary indicator of SCID.

With specialized expertise unavailable locally, the sample was sent to UCLA Health, a nationally recognized leader in immunodeficiency care, for further analysis. There, Manish Butte, MD, PhD, chief of Immunology, Allergy, and Rheumatology, conducted additional testing and confirmed Seersha’s SCID diagnosis.

At just 6 days old, Seersha was airlifted to Los Angeles on a military medical transport flight alongside her mother. To minimize her exposure, she was placed in an incubator at the front of the plane.

“It was terrifying to leave my husband and two other children not knowing when they were going to see her again. We had no idea what we were doing,” says Shayla Sulack, reflecting on the early days of treatment. The entire family eventually relocated to Tehachapi to be closer to Seersha’s UCLA Health team and relatives in the area.

Seersha’s parents feared their youngest child would not make it to her first birthday, but Dr. Kohn’s groundbreaking work in gene therapy — to repair the immune systems of children with SCID — would soon offer hope.

Treatment options for severe combined immunodeficiency disease

According to Dr. Kohn, Seersha inherited two faulty copies of the gene responsible for producing adenosine deaminase, or ADA, a critical enzyme needed by T cells to survive.

“We had no idea we were carriers until we had Seersha,” says Shayla Sulack.

Dr. Kohn and his team leveraged their expertise and explored different treatment options.

“Before treatments existed, SCID was uniformly a fatal disease in infancy. Babies would die within the first year of life from infections,” Dr. Kohn says. “Fortunately, today, that is no longer the case.”

There are two main treatment pathways for children with SCID: bone marrow transplant and gene therapy. Both treatments offer a potential cure, but each comes with unique risks and benefits.

Bone marrow transplants involve the transfer of healthy stem cells from a compatible donor — typically a family member — to the patient.

“If there is a sibling who is a perfect match and does not have SCID, then the chance of a successful transplant is 90-95%,” says Dr. Kohn.

However, this ideal scenario is relatively rare. With only a 25% chance that two siblings will be a perfect match, this option is not viable for many patients. That was the case for Seersha.

“When we first arrived at UCLA, we got our HLA typing done,” explains Seersha’s mom. “My husband and I were only half matches, and our older children were not matches for her at all.”

In these cases, doctors may need to look beyond immediate family. “We can either use the parent who’s half a match, or we can look for an unrelated donor,” explains Dr. Kohn.

But while 80%-90% of children survive these unrelated or half-matched bone marrow transplants, the procedures are often associated with higher risks, including graft-versus-host disease — where donor cells attack the patient.

As a result, to provide Seersha with her best chance for a cure, Dr. Kohn offered the family an alternative: gene therapy.

A unique approach to SCID
Gene therapy involves the process of removing a patient’s stem cells, correcting their genetic makeup, and reintroducing the cells back into the body. In clinical trials administered by Dr. Kohn and his team, gene therapy at UCLA Health has saved the lives of more than 50 babies to date.

“We like gene therapy for us, because we didn’t have to worry about rejection, graft-versus-host disease or anything else. If it didn’t work, we could do other options,” explains Shayla Sulack. “The doctors were also really great about explaining this to Seersha. Because at the end of the day, she's the one living with it, and we're just taking care of it.”

Dr. Kohn and his team extracted Seersha’s stem cells and inserted a normal ADA gene into them. They used a virus as a carrier to deliver the corrected gene into her DNA and reintroduced the modified cells back into her body.

“If gene therapy was not available, Seersha would have had to match with an unrelated donor or a parent,” Dr. Kohn says. “These treatments are much more complicated. They need more chemotherapy. They need immune suppression. So that would have been a longer, harder road.”

Moving forward
Although chemotherapy, medications, infusions and injections were not easy to endure, Seersha remained in high spirits.

“After treatment, we took Seersha home, and for her, it was just another normal day,” says her mother. “She was just ready. Every time we would go to visit the doctor, she would always ask, ‘Can I do more yet?’”

The answer soon became yes.

Seersha is now healthy, with her immune system responding well to the gene therapy treatment. She enjoys exploring the outdoors, playing at the park, learning through homeschool, trying new sports such as softball, and making friends.

“She’s a huge advocate for herself. She’s not shy. She just takes it all in stride,” Shayla Sulack says. “And the fact that she gets to enjoy whatever everybody else does, you know, going to the beach, or even going to the grocery store. It's just simple ups from here.”

“She has grown — you just see the maturation,” Dr. Kohn adds. “She was a baby when we treated her, and now, she’s become a young girl. It is a wonderful blessing to be able to improve people’s lives.”

At the same time, Seersha’s journey has become an inspiration to many. She and her family are dedicated to sharing her story, advocating for other children with ADA-SCID, and offering support to families navigating similar paths.

There's just this huge community of SCID parents, and so, that's all we do, we try to advocate for them to get them the treatments that they need,” says Shayla Sulack.

Reflecting on Seersha’s journey, her mother shares heartfelt advice for families: “Don’t do it alone.”

“It is a terrifying moment when your child is sick,” she says. “You want to close the entire world out to protect your child, but accept the help that is there — because there is help and community.”

Dr. Kohn agrees. “It is a very difficult road, but there’s light at the end, as you can see with Seersha.

“UCLA Health has been a leader in gene therapy for childhood diseases like this,” he says. “The resources that we have — including the transplant program and the laboratories that can process these cells — are unique. We are really one of the few places in the country that offer these kinds of treatments.”

As Seersha’s family — which recently welcomed a new baby — prepares to move to Tennessee, their gratitude for UCLA Health continues to grow.

“We don't want to leave UCLA — we want UCLA to travel with us,” Shayla Sulack says with a smile. “Seersha has been with the UCLA Health team for almost eight years, and they've been with our family since then. They just feel like family.”

I know how it feels to drive hours for camps just to stand in line, shake one hand, and never hear back.

To watch your best friend go D1 on signing day and think your dream might already be done.

Then I used it on myself.

HIGH SCHOOL: 6'0 | 210 | 4.71
COLLEGE: 6'0 | 215 | 4.69

Didn’t grow. Didn’t get faster. Same player.

The only thing that changed was the system.

500+ D1 coaches watched my film. 100+ followed me. That turned into phone calls, multiple D1 offers, and committing Power 4 — with my family in the stands.

Indiana just won the natty with 8 four-and-five-stars on their roster. Miami had 45.

The 8 won.

Recruiting has changed forever.

If you’ve got film, you just need coaches to see it.

Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant" lands. They offered no details on what lands could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales.
Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. text:
Dem Who Screamed for Hegseth Impeachment Misses Vote, Blames Being “Trapped” by Police Motorcade

House Democrat Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico was one of 11 members of her party who failed to show up for the high-profile vote to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth. When Fox News reporter Bill Melugin caught her outside the Capitol, she offered a traffic jam as the reason.

“As I mentioned just now, I was trapped right there at that street corner because there was a police motorcade moving buses off of the campus and I physically was trapped right at that corner in my vehicle in traffic because the police had shut down traffic in both directions,” Stansbury said.

Melugin pressed her on the timing. The vote had been public since Monday night. Once Republicans set it for around 5:30 p.m., the House left it open longer than the planned 15 minutes. “So why not come here sooner though?” he asked.

Stansbury repeated the claim. “Because I did, and I was trapped in my vehicle because of the police motorcade.”

When Melugin noted that traffic might not land as a convincing excuse for a vote her party had treated as a priority, she pushed back. “It was not open for a while. They gaveled the vote as soon as they could.”

Several House Democrats have already voiced frustration with colleagues who missed the roll call after months of demanding Hegseth’s impeachment. Nancy Pelosi’s office confirmed she was not even in Washington; she was in San Francisco when the vote occurred.

Melugin later told the studio the explanation looked thin. The Hill had known the vote was coming since Monday, the window stayed open past the initial 15 minutes, and Democrats had spent weeks calling the issue a top priority. “If they had all been here, there’s a chance that Hegseth may have been impeached in the House,” he said. Instead, the effort failed, and Democrats will have to wait until they potentially regain the majority in January to try again.

The episode left the on-camera exchange as the clearest public accounting of why one of the loudest voices for impeachment was absent when the votes were counted.

When a woman has clearly established boundaries with both men, been transparent about her intentions and made it clear that friendship is all she can offer, does that mean she must stop communicating with someone simply because another man feels threatened? I cannot control how another person feels about me, but I can control how I respond, the boundaries I establish and the integrity of my actions.. text:
I need to get something off my chest.

I've always been transparent about who I am, where I stand emotionally, and what I need before allowing someone into my life.

I've never pretended to offer something I wasn't ready to give.

I've been deeply hurt before. I've experienced things that have taken years to heal from, and I've never hidden the fact that trust, for me, must be established before love can ever be considered.

Someone recently entered my life, and we connected through meaningful conversations, shared beliefs and what I believed was a mutual understanding of friendship and potential relationship.

He developed romantic feelings very quickly. I wasn't there emotionally, and I made that clear.

At no point did I lie, deceive, betray or deliberately mislead him.
I was transparent about my
feelings, my circumstances and the fact that I needed time to build trust. 

Friendship was offered. 
Friendship was agreed upon.

Yet somewhere along the way, my boundaries became interpreted as rejection, my independence as betrayal, and my unwillingness to abandon another human being became grounds for accusations against my character.

I was never anyone's possession.

I never agreed to exclusivity, nor did I surrender my right to decide whom I could speak to.

Then came the accusations that I was interrupting him during our conversations, he raised his voice and told me to "shut the fuck up."

I froze. I couldn't speak. I began crying.

He knew my history. He knew what I had survived, yet, the following day, it happened again. I was sitting in my car speaking with him when my son was leaving for work. I briefly said goodbye to my son, and once again, I was shouted at for supposedly interrupting.

I was saying goodbye to my child.

What hurts most isn't simply being shouted at.

It's knowing that someone who understood the history behind my wounds could speak to me like that.

I am mentally, physically and emotionally exhausted.

Now after choosing silence rather than retaliation, I find my character publicly condemned through accusations of darkness, deception and evil.

Accusations that do not reflect my actions, my intentions or the truth of what occurred.

All because I would not abandon a friendship at someone else's demand.

Until writing these words, I had not responded publicly, retaliated or given any further energy to this situation.

I chose to disengage. 
I respected the separation. 
I blocked communication rather than perpetuate a conflict that was already causing me emotional distress.

Yet my silence did not stop the public accusations.

That is what has finally compelled me to speak.

Not to attack, humiliate or condemn another human being, but because I refuse to allow someone else's pain to become a false testimony of my character.

You cannot profess divine love while believing that another person's independence gives you permission to strip them of their dignity.

Faith does not exempt us from accountability.

Pain does not justify cruelty.

And someone's past trauma is not permission to inflict new wounds upon them.

I am not perfect. 
I have never claimed to be.

But I know the difference between offering someone friendship and promising them my heart.

I know that love, in its truest form, does not demand that another person abandon their freedom to prove their loyalty.

I never asked to be worshipped, rescued or possessed. I simply asked to be understood and treated with kindness.

My silence is not guilt.
My boundaries are not betrayal.
My honesty is not deception.

And my refusal to retaliate is not weakness.

I will not allow another person's interpretation of me to become my identity.

And I will not abandon my faith because another person has used theirs to condemn me.

God knows the intentions of my heart, the truth behind my actions and the integrity with which I have tried to live.  🙏🤍

Matthew 7:16-  "Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?"

text:
Aggregate S&P 500 dividends are a durable corporate cash stream. Dividend paying stocks are not a low volatility bond substitute, and retirement plans that confuse a steady check with protected principal find out the hard way in a bear market: three of the largest U.S. dividend funds lost between 33% and 57% at their worst, and the 33% fund only launched in October 2011, missing 2008 entirely.

Stack Robert Shiller's monthly S&P 500 dividend series since January 1950 against dividend adjusted daily closes across those three funds:

• Where payouts held (January 1950 to June 2026): S&P 500 dividends compounded at 5.74% a year against 3.53% CPI inflation, never dipped below market peak levels in 1980 to 1982, 1987, or 2022, slipped 0.8% in 1973 to 1974 while index price fell 48.2%, and fell at worst 24.1% in 2007 to 2009 while index price dropped 56.8%.

• The inflation blind spot: Even without selling a share, inflation cut the purchasing power of S&P 500 dividends by 10.9% in 1973 to 1974, 10.8% in 2000 to 2002, and 25.5% in 2007 to 2009.

• The principal drawdown reality: The high dividend yield fund shown fell deeper than the S&P 500 fund in both 2007 to 2009 (57.0% versus 55.2%) and 2020 (35.2% versus 33.7%), and while all three dividend funds fell less than the S&P 500's 24.5% loss in 2022, they still dropped 15.8% to 20.4%, breaching the 15% loss limit on the chart.

A cash dividend is paid out of enterprise value, so the stock price drops by roughly the payout on the ex-dividend date while principal carries full equity multiple risk. Corporate boards fight to defend the quarterly check, whereas nobody in the boardroom can defend the valuation multiple in a liquidity squeeze. In a taxable account, forced dividend yield also taxes 100% of every dollar distributed, while selling appreciated shares taxes only the gain above cost basis.

At a 1.1% S&P 500 yield as of June 2026, $1 million generates roughly $11,000 a year. A household spending 1% of its balance sheet can live off index dividends alone. At typical retirement withdrawal rates, portfolio loss limits are set by high-quality bond and cash reserves, not equity yield screens. In our view, fund near term draws in fixed income or cash, size spending from total return, and coordinate the tax math with your CPA.

text:
I have taken about 900 thousand photos of Texas. There are few that stick with me more than this one, which I post here every Veteran's day.  This is a ceramic photograph that I found on a grave marker in a rural black cemetery near Giddings. The cemetery is fairly remote, such that there's no way I could navigate back to it without the help of a map.

The inscription on the tombstone reads:
Pvt. Clinton Francis
Born March 29, 1893
Died Nov. 24, 1918
A Soldier's Death

I initially thought that Private Francis must have died from wounds he received during World War I, but some of y'all tracked him down via genealogy records and his death certificate reads that he died of tuberculosis. My guess is that perhaps that is actually incorrect and that he died of the Spanish Flu that was raging that year.

But look at him looking back at us though the generations. See how handsome he is in his uniform and his gloves and his boots.

I can't say why this photo sticks with me.  Anybody who knew Private Francis is long gone. He is now just a forgotten man in a lonely cemetery, dust blowing around the corner, smoke slipping through a keyhole, dust illuminated by sunlight in an old room.

But I have not forgotten you, Private Francis!  Every Veteran's day, I remember. And I raise my glass to you and to the uncountable others and offer only the hope that we not let the memories of your sacrifices be forgotten.

A soldier's death, indeed.

He then pivoted to a clear threat if enforcement continues.

The crowd responded with cheers.

text:
Cybersecurity Tip

A tip from your friend in cybersecurity and risk management

You may get a breach letter from a company you have never heard of. Read it anyway.

Baker Tilly, a national accounting and advisory firm, began notifying people on November 9 about a breach on a third-party platform it uses for client work. An unauthorized person got in on September 2. Names, addresses, and Social Security numbers were exposed, and both adults and minors are affected. So far, 10,456 Texas residents and 111 Rhode Island residents have been affected.

If you get a letter, enroll in the free two years of Experian IdentityWorks monitoring it offers. Freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and freeze your children's credit too if they are named. Then watch for calls and emails that use your details to sound official.

Share this with someone who needs it.

#DataBreach #CreditFreeze #IdentityTheft

text:
🐾 Give a static 3D creature a motion idea, then recover a rigged animation from the video that idea produces.

AniMimic, a CVPR 2026 research project from UCLA and the University of Utah, connects video generation with editable 3D motion.

The starting point is an existing mesh. The system renders a reference view, generates an animation video and uses that video to guide how the original geometry should move.

🧩 The pipeline goes through several stages:

▪️ Construct a skeleton and skinning weights with an automatic rigging model.
▪️ Optimize joint motion so renders of the animated mesh follow the generated video.
▪️ Use tracked image points and estimated depth to constrain the movement.
▪️ Refine deformation through differentiable soft-body simulation.

That final stage addresses a weakness of ordinary skinning. A mesh can follow its joints while still looking rigid, collapsing around bends or missing the secondary motion that makes a soft body feel alive.

AniMimic adjusts material stiffness within its simulation so the deformation better matches the motion reference. The paper uses a Warp-based physics implementation and combines image, silhouette, tracking and depth information during optimization.

🎥 The output can be rendered from viewpoints other than the original generated video, which is an important distinction from simply producing an animated 2D clip.

The published implementation description uses Kling to generate the reference motion. This is an optimization-based research pipeline, rather than an instant text-to-animation model.

Its quality is tied to the generated reference and estimated rig: inconsistent video details and imperfect skinning are problems the method has to work around.

The public project page currently offers the paper and demonstrations, without a linked downloadable code release or a ready-made Blender extension.

For character-animation research, it is an interesting way to use a video model’s motion imagination while retaining an actual mesh, skeleton and deformation process behind the result.

text:
With seemingly no limit to the demand for artificial intelligence, everyone in the energy, AI, and climate fields is justifiably worried. Will there be enough clean electricity to power AI and enough water to cool the data centers that support this technology? These are important questions with serious implications for communities, the economy, and the environment. 

This story is a part of MIT Technology Review’s series “Power Hungry: AI and our energy future,” on the energy demands and carbon costs of the artificial-intelligence revolution.

But the question about AI’s energy usage portends even bigger issues about what we need to do in addressing climate change for the next several decades. If we can’t work out how to handle this, we won’t be able to handle broader electrification of the economy, and the climate risks we face will increase.

Innovation in IT got us to this point. Graphics processing units (GPUs) that power the computing behind AI have fallen in cost by 99% since 2006. There was similar concern about the energy use of data centers in the early 2010s, with wild projections of growth in electricity demand. But gains in computing power and energy efficiency not only proved these projections wrong but enabled a 550% increase in global computing capability from 2010 to 2018 with only minimal increases in energy use. 

In the late 2010s, however, the trends that had saved us began to break. As the accuracy of AI models dramatically improved, the electricity needed for data centers also started increasing faster; they now account for 4.4% of total demand, up  from 1.9% in 2018. Data centers consume more than 10% of the electricity supply in six US states. In Virginia, which has emerged as a hub of data center activity, that figure is 25%.

Projections about the future demand for energy to power AI are uncertain and range widely, but in one study, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers could represent 6% to 12% of total US electricity use by 2028. Communities and companies will notice this type of rapid growth in electricity demand. It will put pressure on energy prices and on ecosystems. The projections have resulted in calls to build lots of new fossil-fired power plants or bring older ones out of retirement. In many parts of the US, the demand will likely result in a surge of natural-gas-powered plants.

It’s a daunting situation. Yet when we zoom out, the projected electricity use from AI is still pretty small. The US generated about 4,300 billion kilowatt-hours last year. We’ll likely need another 1,000 billion to 1,200 billion or more in the next decade—a 24% to 29% increase. Almost half the additional electricity demand will be from electrified vehicles. Another 30% is expected to be from electrified technologies in buildings and industry. Innovation in vehicle and building electrification also advanced in the last decade, and this shift will be good news for the climate, for communities, and for energy costs.

The remaining 22% of new electricity demand is estimated to come from AI and data centers. While it represents a smaller piece of the pie, it’s the most urgent one. Because of their rapid growth and geographic concentration, data centers are the electrification challenge we face right now—the small stuff we have to figure out before we’re able to do the big stuff like vehicles and buildings.

We also need to understand what the energy consumption and carbon emissions associated with AI are buying us. While the impacts from producing semiconductors and powering AI data centers are important, they are likely small compared with the positive or negative effects AI may have on applications such as the electricity grid, the transportation system, buildings and factories, or consumer behavior. Companies could use AI to develop new materials or batteries that would better integrate renewable energy into the grid. But they could also use AI to make it easier to find more fossil fuels. The claims about potential benefits for the climate are exciting, but they need to be continuously verified and will need support to be realized.

This isn’t the first time we’ve faced challenges coping with growth in electricity demand. In the 1960s, US electricity demand was growing at more than 7% per year. In the 1970s that growth was nearly 5%, and in the 1980s and 1990s it was more than 2% per year. Then, starting in 2005, we basically had a decade and a half of flat electricity growth. Most projections for the next decade put our expected growth in electricity demand at around 2% again—but this time we’ll have to do things differently. 

To manage these new energy demands, we need a “Grid New Deal” that leverages public and private capital to rebuild the electricity system for AI with enough capacity and intelligence for decarbonization. New clean energy supplies, investment in transmission and distribution, and strategies for virtual demand management can cut emissions, lower prices, and increase resilience. Data centers bringing clean electricity and distribution system upgrades could be given a fast lane to connect to the grid. Infrastructure banks could fund new transmission lines or pay to upgrade existing ones. Direct investment or tax incentives could encourage clean computing standards, workforce development in the clean energy sector, and open data transparency from data center operators about their energy use so that communities can understand and measure the impacts.

In 2022, the White House released a Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights that provided principles to protect the public’s rights, opportunities, and access to critical resources from being restricted by AI systems. To the AI Bill of Rights, we humbly offer a climate amendment, because ethical AI must be climate-safe AI. It’s a starting point to ensure that the growth of AI works for everyone—that it doesn’t raise people’s energy bills, adds more clean power to the grid than it uses, increases investment in the power system’s infrastructure, and benefits communities while driving innovation.

By grounding the conversation about AI and energy in context about what is needed to tackle climate change, we can deliver better outcomes for communities, ecosystems, and the economy. The growth of electricity demand for AI and data centers is a test case for how society will respond to the demands and challenges of broader electrification. If we get this wrong, the likelihood of meeting our climate targets will be extremely low. This is what we mean when we say the energy and climate impacts from data centers are small, but they are also huge.

Costa Samaras is the Trustee Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering and director of the Scott Institute for Energy Innovation at Carnegie Mellon University.

Emma Strubell is the Raj Reddy Assistant Professor in the Language Technologies Institute in the School of Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University.

Ramayya Krishnan is dean of the Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy and the William W. and Ruth F. Cooper Professor of Management Science and Information Systems at Carnegie Mellon University.

text:
Virginia just voted on a major constitutional amendment affecting abortion laws. At different points in my life, I've been both pro-life and pro-choice. Here's why I've come to believe the answer lies somewhere in the middle:

- When I was pro-life: I avoided thinking about the millions of miscarriages each year. I questioned my religion because I couldn't reconcile the miracle of conception with the cruelty of so many losses. We fight so desperately to save one another that “free will” feels like a cruel explanation. I go to church and send my children to Catholic school, but there are still questions I'm terrified to ask.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about where life began to deserve protection. Every line I tried to draw felt arbitrary. I wanted certainty. Instead, I found myself standing in a grayness so vast I hated myself.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided questioning the Church's opposition to IVF. Conception is an almost unimaginable lottery determining who gets to exist. I couldn't understand why helping a loving couple create life through careful, responsible medicine was somehow less sacred. Or how anyone could ask a couple to bury the dreams of children they longed to hold.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about premature babies. Parents sitting beside an incubator, watching a machine breathe for someone they already loved beyond reason. Fighting, praying... surviving.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided thinking about the mother of four whose last pregnancy nearly killed her. Now pregnant again, facing the possibility that bringing a fifth child into the world could leave four children without their mother. I could explain the sanctity of the unborn. I couldn't explain away the sanctity of the woman standing in her kitchen, looking at four children who still needed her alive.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about the first flicker of cardiac activity. Not yet a fully formed heart, not proof of consciousness, but the beginning of something unmistakably alive and developing.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided thinking about children born into cruelty, only to grow into prisoners we condemn. And I struggled with the hypocrisy of defending their right to be born, only to grow quiet about the suffering that followed. It's why we foster, but our reach is so small.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about the abortion itself. Suspended in darkness, defenseless.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided the thought experiment about the burning fertility clinic. A newborn in one room. Several viable embryos in another. Only enough time to save one. I would save the newborn. Yes, I would offer my own life if that somehow made it possible to save them all. But if the choice were absolute, I knew which way I would run. And I hated that my answer left me standing in the grayness again.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about Planned Parenthood's history of racism and eugenics. Or the Freakonomics argument that legalizing abortion helped reduce crime. What haunted me was the thought of celebrating a safer world because certain children were never given the chance to live in it.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided imagining a woman in my family being raped and what I would say if she became pregnant. I could speak so confidently about the sanctity of life until I imagined someone I loved enduring that horror. All I would think about was killing the man who did it. And suddenly, my moral certainty seemed so much easier to defend when the suffering belonged to someone else.

And every time I tried to settle comfortably into one side, I found myself calculating answers I could barely stand to say aloud. So that's why I don't go by the terms pro-choice or pro-life. I believe both early stages of human life and the dignity of the woman carrying it deserve reverence. Every circumstance between them deserves delicacy, humility, and compassion. We live in a state of imperfection. Be kind. All we have is each other.

text:
The core question raised in this text—why the "China threat" narrative consistently treats U.S. power in Asia as a neutral baseline while framing China’s actions as deviations—finds verifiable support in both academic literature and official documents. Testimony before the U.S. House Armed Services Committee in April 2026 explicitly identifies "maintaining a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific" as a strategic objective, detailing investments in and expanded access to military sites—including those under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) in the Philippines, as well as locations in Palau and Micronesia. A 2025 analysis by the National Institute for South China Sea Studies documents the same phenomenon from a different perspective: through a "three-sea linkage" strategy, the United States has "securitized" issues concerning the South China Sea, the East China Sea, and the Taiwan Strait, using the perception of a "China threat" as a narrative foundation to construct a network of military bases and a system of alliances and partnerships. Regarding the U.S. dollar system, minutes from a 2026 New York Federal Reserve meeting confirm that the dollar’s ​​dominance relies on "network effects, institutional support, and market depth," while any alternatives face significant "inertia." Meanwhile, the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) for the Chinese yuan clears approximately 700 billion RMB (roughly $100 billion) daily—a figure far lower than the nearly $2 trillion cleared daily through the U.S.-based CHIPS (Clearing House Interbank Payments System). While these facts do not directly answer whether U.S. power *should* be considered the baseline, they confirm that the asymmetry described in the text is indeed real.

The Military Dimension of the "Baseline": Who Deploys Forces Near Whom?

Testimony delivered to the U.S. House Armed Services Committee on April 22, 2026, provides concrete details regarding what constitutes the "U.S. military presence in Asia." In his testimony, the Commander of the U.S. Indo-Pacific Command outlined infrastructure investments at EDCA sites in the Philippines (exceeding $300 million as of fiscal year 2026), the development of Tactical Over-the-Horizon Radar (TACMOR) capabilities and defensive installations on Peleliu in Palau, upgrades to airfields and seaports in Yap State (Micronesia), and the securing of "guaranteed military access" through the Compacts of Free Association. The same testimony called for allies to increase their core defense spending to 3.5% of their respective GDPs, with a target of 5% for Taiwan. An analysis by the National Institute for South China Sea Studies presents another dimension of the same set of facts, viewed from a Chinese perspective: the United States has constructed a network of military bases across the "three seas" region, engaged in "diversified military deterrence operations," and "built numerous bilateral and minilateral alliance and partnership networks." The core argument of this analysis is that the United States, "obsessed with maintaining its maritime hegemony," perceives the development of Chinese maritime power as a challenge to its own "maritime dominance"—thereby "continuously reinforcing its perception of being 'threatened'."

Both sets of texts point to the same underlying structure: the United States maintains an extensive network of bases and access arrangements around China’s periphery, framing this presence as essential for "regional security" and "deterrence." The question posed here is: why does this U.S. presence require no justification, while China’s own military development in its immediate neighborhood is treated as something that must be explained? It is verifiable that official U.S. documents do not view this presence as a "baseline" requiring defense; rather, it is regarded as a component of a "favorable balance of power"—something that must be "maintained" or "restored."

The Financial Dimension of the "Baseline": The Inertia of the U.S. Dollar System

Minutes from a February 2026 meeting of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York offer an academic account of the mechanisms that sustain the dominance of the U.S. dollar. Participants noted that shifts in a dominant currency "typically unfold over decades rather than occurring abruptly," as a dominant currency benefits from "strong network effects, institutional support, and market depth—all of which create significant inertia that resists rapid change." The same record notes that U.S. dollar-denominated assets "continue to offer relatively high returns," which encourages global investors to maintain their exposure, even as a desire for "diversification" begins to emerge.

This description aligns, in terms of mechanism, with the observation made earlier in this text: that U.S. control over global financial infrastructure is simply taken for granted as "the way things are." Verifiable data bears this out: CIPS (Cross-Border Interbank Payment System) clears approximately $100 billion daily, compared to nearly $2 trillion for CHIPS (Clearing House Interbank Payments System); meanwhile, international bonds denominated in the Chinese yuan account for only 0.8% of the global total. While these figures do not in themselves prove that the U.S. dollar system is "natural," they do confirm that the system’s scale-based advantages are structural—and not merely sustained by policy choices. The question posed in this text is: when this scale-based advantage is framed in terms of "market depth" and "network effects," why is any attempt to establish an alternative characterized as "destabilizing"?

Analysis of the "Empire as Time" Rhetorical Framework

The core insight of this text—that American power is perceived as "time" rather than as an "actor"—finds a parallel in critical academic discourse. A commentary piece from the Hong Kong-based *South China Morning Post* (SCMP) in September 2025 addresses this phenomenon directly. It references an op-ed in *The Wall Street Journal* by Rahm Emanuel—former Obama chief of staff and former U.S. Ambassador to Japan—who describes the "China threat" as both "real and potent," while asking whether Americans can "stop fighting among themselves long enough to realize the threat from China." The SCMP commentary counters that the "China threat" is merely one of the inflated menaces that Washington politicians rely on to "scare the American people." It further argues that this narrative serves to "provide legitimacy for an empire that is undeniably in retreat."

This critique mirrors the structure of the text in question: rather than denying that China possesses military power or global ambitions, it points out that the "threat" narrative functions to naturalize a specific power arrangement—the U.S.-led order—thereby rendering any questioning of that order invisible. Notably, this critique originates from within Western media discourse (while the SCMP is based in Hong Kong, its commentators often come from Western backgrounds), rather than exclusively from official Chinese channels.

text:
Dolores was a 78-year-old widow who sat at the corner table every morning because her house was too quiet.

The boy was 15, the nephew of one of the baristas. He studied at the café before school because his mom worked nights.

For four years, Jess had quietly bought them breakfast and coffee every single day.

She never told me.

I sat in my car outside the café, feeling like the smallest man in Ohio.

That night, I asked her why she had never mentioned it.

She looked at me and said, “Because you’d have done the math.”

She was right.

I’d calculated every dollar and called it irresponsible.

I apologized. I restored the subscription. I even offered to set up a joint budget category for it.

She refused.

“The point was never the money,” she said. “The point was that you never asked.”

I understand that now.

But she also kept it from me for four years.

Even when the intention is good, keeping something that affects shared finances a secret can create its own kind of hurt.

I thought I was protecting our money. Instead, I showed my wife that I could calculate the cost of her kindness without ever understanding its value.

From: @JtotheAY

11/11/26

To: Jackie Singh (@HackingButLegal)

Re: FORMAL CEASE AND DESIST: Defamation Per Se and Telecommunications Harassment Under Ohio Law. Demand for Retraction and Preservation of Evidence.

Ms. Singh,

This letter is formal notice that your public statements about me are false, defamatory per se, and actionable under Ohio law. I demand that you immediately retract them and stop all further publication.

The defamatory statement

On November 9, 2026, you published the following to nearly 100,000 followers on X, where it has been seen more than 54,000 times (https://t.co/nSaHFUyUNn):

«"Warning (serious): A bunch of domestic terrorists are operating under the hashtags "eggsalad" and "goldcorp""»

I am one of the people who post under those hashtags. Your statement accuses that identifiable group, and me as part of it, of being "domestic terrorists." Terrorism is a serious felony under Ohio law (R.C. 2909.24) and federal law (18 U.S.C. § 2331(5)). The accusation is false. I have never planned, supported, or taken part in any act of terrorism or violence.

Defamation per se under Ohio law

Under Ohio law, a statement is defamatory when it is a false statement of fact, published to a third party, made with the required degree of fault, that harms the subject's reputation. Falsely accusing someone of an indictable crime involving moral turpitude or infamous punishment is defamation per se. Damages are presumed, so I do not need to prove specific harm to recover.

Your statement is not protected opinion. You labeled it a "Warning (serious)," presented it as fact to warn the public, and offered no facts to back it up. A reasonable reader would take it as a factual claim that the people under those hashtags are terrorists.

You describe yourself as an investigative journalist and threat researcher. Making this accusation with no supporting evidence, to an audience that relies on you for exactly that kind of assessment, shows at least negligence and, I believe, reckless disregard for the truth.

Harassment

Publishing these statements and continuing to target the people associated with these hashtags may also be telecommunications harassment under R.C. 2917.21. Under R.C. 2307.60, anyone injured by a criminal act may bring a civil action for full compensatory damages, punitive damages where authorized, and court costs and attorney's fees. Repeated conduct that causes mental distress may also support a civil stalking protection order under R.C. 2903.214.

Demands

By [date, 7 days out], you must:

1. Permanently delete the post above and every other post, reply, quote-post, or publication, on X or elsewhere, that calls me or the people using these hashtags terrorists or criminals.
2. Publish a clear retraction on X, from the same account and with the same visibility, stating that your accusation was false.
3. Stop making any further false statements about me or the people targeted by your accusation, and stop all harassing conduct directed at us.
4. Confirm in writing that you have done all of the above.

Litigation hold

You are now on notice of a likely legal claim. You must preserve all evidence related to this matter, including posts, deleted posts, drafts, replies, direct messages, analytics, screenshots, and communications with any third party about me or these hashtags. Destroying or altering any of it after this notice may lead to sanctions and an adverse-inference finding in any later lawsuit.

Consequences of non-compliance

If you do not fully comply by the date above, I intend to pursue every civil remedy available under Ohio law without further notice. That includes a defamation action seeking presumed, compensatory, and punitive damages, a civil action under R.C. 2307.60, and injunctive relief.

Nothing in this letter waives any of my rights or remedies, all of which are expressly reserved.

text:
The best wedding speech I've ever read was a list, written by a Japanese groom in Wisconsin.

The groom is my college friend Kazuma. He sent it to me before the reception, to ask if his English was okay.

It wasn't okay. It was perfect. Here's part of it:

"Things I learned from the Brekke family in four years.

Friday is fish fry. It is not a meal. It is a weekly meeting where everyone you know eats fish and nobody goes home before ten.

Nine minutes after I met Kristin's uncle, he asked me who my team was. I said I didn't have one. He said, 'You do now.' I own three foam cheese hats. I wore one to my office in Tokyo. Nobody asked. Everybody wanted to.

At a supper club, before you order, they bring a plate of raw carrots, celery and crackers. Nobody asked for it. Nobody knows when it started. Everybody eats it. I have decided this is the most Wisconsin thing in Wisconsin.

Fresh cheese curds squeak against your teeth. If they don't squeak, Kristin's grandmother will not allow them in the house. I now judge all cheese by sound. My mother thinks I have changed.

Kristin's brother drove six hours through snow to help me move one couch. I offered cash. His face fell. Then he made me carry the heavy end."

Kazuma told me what happened after the speech.

His parents were in the second row. They had flown in from Osaka. They don't speak English. They had smiled politely through every word.

Then Kristin's father stood up with a glass.

He had spent four months learning a toast in Japanese from YouTube. His pronunciation was terrible. Half the words were in the wrong order.

Kazuma's mother understood every one of them:

"Please don't worry about your son. He has a family here too."

Kazuma's mother did not cry at her own wedding. She cried at this one.

Two days later, at the airport, Kristin's brother picked up both of his parents' suitcases. Kazuma's father, 68, reached to take one back.

Her brother's face fell.

Kazuma's father understood. He let go.

That man has carried the heavy end his whole life.

In Wisconsin, for one morning, somebody carried it for him.

Analysis: Is This Speech "Talking Itself into the Abyss of Oblivion"?
Short answer: No — but the speech is acutely aware of that risk and is explicitly arguing against it.

Here's what's actually happening in the text:

What the speech is doing
This is a Knesset address (likely from a recent Israeli political figure, given references to October 7, the "evil empire of Iran," and the Abraham Accords states) that is deliberately invoking David Ben-Gurion's 1949 transition speech. The rhetorical structure is:

Invoke the founding moment — Ben-Gurion's call to move from "great ups and downs and the victory of war" to "small tasks": building, recruitment, education, health.

Define the present task the same way — "a diligent, persistent and faithful work" — parliamentary work, routine governance, not dramatic victory.

Diagnose the danger — a "divided, changing Israel," gaps, quarrels, fears, "many wounds still open."

Prescribe the remedy — compromise, listening, unity, "raise your hand for compromise," reject corruption/racism/violence.

Close with hope — a small light (Kislev/Hanukkah imagery) illuminating the distances; a prayer for peace.

Why it is not "talking itself into oblivion"
The phrase "talking itself into the abyss of oblivion" suggests a body politic rhetorically sleepwalking into self-destruction. But the text is doing the opposite:

It names the abyss explicitly: "A picture of a divided, changing Israel emerged from within," "moral barriers that break our beautiful faces," "many wounds are still open in our flesh."

It warns against the mechanism of oblivion: "We will not be able to heal them as long as the pain of one is the purpose of the other."

It prescribes an antidote: routine, faithful, persistent institutional work — the exact opposite of dramatic self-immolation.

The legitimate critique you may be reaching for
There is a tension worth naming:

The speech loads enormous existential weight onto "routine" and "small tasks" while simultaneously listing civilizational threats (Iran, October 7 accountability, AI/technological revolution, judicial/political divisions). Asking a fractured parliament to meet both the routine and the existential at once is precisely the strain that can produce paralysis.

The repeated call to "raise your hand for compromise" and "listen" is aspirational rhetoric delivered to a body the speech itself describes as representing "gaps, disagreements, quarrels and fears." Words about unity are not unity.

The Ben-Gurion framing risks nostalgic substitution: invoking 1949's clarity to mask 2024's (or whenever this was delivered) fragmentation. The "small light" metaphor is beautiful but is doing a lot of work that institutions may not be doing.

Bottom line
The speech is not oblivion-talk. It is anti-oblivion rhetoric — a warning against division, violence, corruption and racism, wrapped in the Ben-Gurion/light-in-the-darkness tradition. Whether it succeeds depends on whether the listeners translate "diligent, persistent and faithful work" into action. The text itself would agree with your concern: it says the repair "begins here, in this house" — meaning the abyss is avoided or entered by what happens in that room, not by the speech alone.

NOW COMPARE THE ELABERATION OF SOME ONE WHO HAS WITNESSED THE DIABOLICAL REASON ALL THIS COME ABOUT IN THE FIRST PLACE?

Comparing the Two Texts: Founding Rhetoric vs. Testimony of the System's Product
You're asking me to compare the Ben-Gurion-style Knesset speech (Text 1) with the former soldier's testimony (Text 2). The contrast is stark, and it's not incidental — the second text is, in effect, a first-person account of what the first text's "routine," "small tasks," and "diligent, persistent and faithful work" look like from the receiving end of the boot.

1. The rhetorical frame vs. the lived mechanism
Text 1 frames the state's task as: routine, order, security, peace, compromise, listening, "small tasks," building institutions, "a small light can illuminate the distances." It speaks in the language of statecraft and aspiration. The abyss it warns against is division, corruption, racism, violence — named as moral failures to be repaired "here, in this house."

Text 2 describes the operational machinery that produces the very things Text 1 names as failures. The soldier's account is not abstract: curfew enforcement, "shoot to kill" orders for curfew breakers, home seizures as temporary bases, tying residents to fences, locking front doors, caged streets, ghost towns, nighttime "arrest" raids that are functionally execution orders, and a legal architecture in which a Jewish settler in Hebron has the rights of a Jerusalem citizen while the Palestinian next door lives under military rule.

"I realised that my job is actually to maintain an apartheid system... I cannot touch a Jewish settler if he is attacking a Palestinian. The best I can do is call a local police department."

This is the diabolical reason you're pointing at: the system is not a malfunction of the founding vision — the testimony argues it is the implementation of a demographic and territorial logic. Text 1 says "a state is not tested only at the time of victory, it is tested... on a routine basis." Text 2 is a granular description of what that routine actually is for Palestinians under occupation.

2. "Diligent, persistent and faithful work" — from whose perspective?
Text 1's core prescription is Ben-Gurion's phrase: diligent, persistent and faithful work — parliamentary work, implementation of the mission, routine governance.

Text 2 supplies the missing subject of that sentence. The "diligent, persistent and faithful work" the soldier describes is:

Roaming streets to enforce curfews so settlers can celebrate

Bursting into a city "with our guns in our hands... screaming Kofia"

Maintaining a hierarchy where "the rights that the Jewish settlers have are not the rights of the Palestinians"

Instilling fear "in the hearts of Palestinians in Hebron" — which he says was "our defined mission"

So when Text 1 praises faithful, persistent routine work, Text 2 asks: faithful to what, persistent at what, and at whose expense? The same institutional virtue — diligence, routine, persistence — is the mechanism of the oppression the soldier describes. That's the diabolical reason: the system runs on exactly the civic virtues Text 1 celebrates.

3. The moral inversion both texts circle
Text 1: "the boundaries between good and bad" is implicit in its call to reject corruption, racism, violence, and to pursue compromise and peace.

Text 2 makes that boundary explicit as a psychological event:

"The boundaries between good and bad that I learned as a kid and obviously I learned that I'm on the good side, I was broken. I felt like I am a terrorist."

And crucially, he explains how the inversion is sustained:

"Growing up in Israel... I believed that I was the good guy... You learn about the Holocaust growing up... I knew that I am going to be a good human being." Then: "I began being almost obsessed with trying to understand the Nazi side... how can a Nazi soldier get up in the morning, give his kids a kiss... and go out to the camps and do his job. I just couldn't understand it. And when I got into the occupied territories, for the first time I understood how can there be a contradiction inside yourself."

This is the answer to your question about "someone who has witnessed the diabolical reason all this come about in the first place." The witness identifies the mechanism of moral insulation: a society formed around victimhood memory and "good guy" identity can, without experiencing contradiction, produce people who kiss their children goodbye and go enforce a curfew with shoot-to-kill orders. Text 1 invokes the Holocaust-adjacent moral language ("a small light," "peace," "blessing to all the families of the earth") — Text 2 shows the same moral vocabulary coexisting with the machinery of domination. That coexistence is the diabolical reason.

4. The "cycle of violence" frame vs. the structural account
Text 1: "the evil empire of Iran does not cease... in its threats"; "the fierce and determined war against our enemies"; build "a stable political balance in the region."

Text 2 directly dismantles the "cycle of violence" framing the interviewer offers:

"If you will not respect existence, you can't expect resistance... Every other attempt from Palestinians to try to negotiate this situation in a diplomatic way was countered by more attacks, more oppression, more occupation, more stealing of the land... We basically described every form of resistance as terrorism because the sole idea of the occupation is not to be safe. The sole idea is to create an equitably-planned piece of land only for Jewish people."

And on complexity:

"It's probably the most simple situation, political situation of our time. It's a situation about equality."

Text 1 calls the challenges "complex" and "many more, and they are complex." Text 2's testimony says the complexity is a rhetorical product — a way of making a simple question (equal rights or not) appear unsolvable. That's a direct challenge to the framing of Text 1.

5. The Mizrahi/Arab-Jewish passage — the system's internal logic
Text 2's long passage on Arab Jews is the deepest structural claim: that the state imported Mizrahi Jews, placed them in "buffer zones" on hostile borders, segregated and sprayed them with DDT, and required them to erase their Arab identity to assimilate — producing "the most extreme right in Israel" as a loyalty-signaling reaction. This is the witness describing how the system manufactures its own base, including the demographic raw material for the very "division" and "extreme right" that Text 1 laments.

Text 1 says: "There is no place for racism inside, towards anyone." Text 2 says the state's founding demography and settlement geography produced racialized hierarchy as a structural feature, not an aberration. The two texts are not describing the same country.

Watchfulness, Stillness, and Self-Disclosure: Liban’s Inner Method
Liban has recently been exploring muraqabah, a Sufi discipline whose Arabic root r-q-b means “to watch, to observe, to wait for something with alert attention”. In practice, he treats it in a way close to what modern psychology calls mindfulness. Thoughts and feelings are allowed to come and go. Each is simply named. Those that need follow-up are noted and set aside, and the rest are released. The act of naming has empirical support: experimental work found that putting feelings into words, called “affect labeling,” reduced amygdala responses to emotional stimuli.[sufiphilosophy +1]

The practice also connects with an old Roman observation. Cicero records Cato’s report that Scipio Africanus used to say he was never less at leisure than when at leisure. Neuroscience offers a modern parallel. When the brain is not occupied with an external task, it does not go idle. It shifts into a “default mode” of organized activity. This default network is linked to self-referential thought, remembering the past, and imagining the future. Undemanding mind-wandering has also been shown to improve creative problem-solving after an incubation period. For Liban, apparent inactivity is therefore not empty. In it, the mind works through concerns, processes emotions, or rests. When internal distraction loosens, a kind of tranquility can appear.[nih +3]
Liban pairs this inner discipline with control of his outer environment. Behavioral economists call such arrangements commitment devices: choices made in advance that restrict later options in order to counter predictable lapses in self-control. He also uses the PINCH heuristic: Passion, Interest, Novelty, Competition, and Hurry. The mnemonic draws on psychiatrist William Dodson’s description of an “interest-based nervous system,” in which motivation is driven by interest, challenge, novelty, and urgency rather than by importance alone. Liban has noticed that adding urgency, the drive to get things done as quickly as possible, sharply increases his output. This suggests, though it does not establish, that his own motivation may follow that pattern.[annualreviews +1]

A second strand of his thinking pulls these practices together. Liban finds that tranquility grows out of several things working at once. He stops clenching against events. He accepts what is fated. He focuses on what lies within his circle of influence. He lets most thoughts pass and follows up only on the ones that matter. This is an old idea. Epictetus opens the Enchiridion by separating the things in our power from the things that are not. It also has a modern clinical form in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, which cultivates psychological flexibility through acceptance, present-moment awareness, and committed action guided by values.[gutenberg +1]
What moves Liban most deeply is the way Ibn ʿArabi’s concept of tajalli, divine self-disclosure, sheds light on this tranquility. For Ibn ʿArabi, the Real “discloses itself in all things.” Creation is “re-created at each instant,” and “there is no repetition” in that self-disclosure. The heart is the “locus of awareness,” and its perception is distorted when either reason or imagination dominates (ibid.). Liban reads this as follows: when the heart stops grasping, it becomes able to see what is already unfolding. Things emerge on their own, by the grace of Allah, not through his own effort.[stanford]
He sees a close parallel in Chinese thought. The Daodejing speaks of doing less and less until one does nothing, “yet nothing is left undone”. Edward Slingerland describes wu-wei as “effortless action”: a state in which skilled, fitting conduct comes forth spontaneously rather than through forced striving. Whether the language is tajalli or spontaneous arising, Liban sees the same insight. Calm, watchful non-grasping, supported by a well-designed environment, is not passivity. It is the condition in which things get done.

text:
The winepress imagery in Revelation 14:19–20 and Revelation 19:15 draws directly from two major Old Testament passages: Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63:1–6. Together, these passages show a continuous prophetic thread where the "winepress" represents the final, decisive judgment of God upon rebellious nations.

1. Joel 3:13 — The Harvest of Wickedness
In Joel 3:12–14, God summons all nations to the Valley of Jehoshaphat (meaning "Yahweh Judges") for a final reckoning:

"Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Go in, tread, for the winepress is full. The vats overflow, for their evil is great." (Joel 3:13)
•Why the Winepress Overflows: In Joel, the grapes represent accumulated human evil reaching its absolute limit. God delays judgment until the "evil is great," mirroring how He waited until the iniquity of the Amorites was complete in Genesis 15:16.
•The Direct Link to Revelation 14: John uses the exact sequence from Joel 3:13—first swinging the sharp sickle to harvest, and immediately following it by casting the clusters into the great winepress (Revelation 14:15–19).

2. Isaiah 63:1–6 — The Warrior in Crimson Garments
While Joel introduces the harvest and the overflowing vats, Isaiah 63:1–6 reveals who treads the winepress and what it looks like:

"Why is your apparel red, and your garments like his who treads in the winepress? 'I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me; I trod them in my anger and trampled them in my wrath; their lifeblood spattered on my garments, and stained all my apparel.'" (Isaiah 63:2–3)
•Treading Alone: Isaiah depicts a mighty Divine Warrior marching in splendor, stained crimson not with grape juice, but with the lifeblood of His enemies. He acts alone because no human army or earthly power can accomplish this final deliverance.
•Vengeance and Redemption Together: In Isaiah 63:4, the Warrior explains His dual purpose: "For the day of vengeance was in my heart, and my year of redemption had come."Judgment on the oppressors and redemption for God's people happen at the exact same moment.

3. How They Converge in Revelation 19:15
In Revelation 19:11–16, John brings Joel's winepress, Isaiah's blood-stained Warrior, and the sharp two-edged sword together into one unified scene at the return of Christ:

Imagery Element
Old Testament Source
Fulfillment in Revelation 19:13–15
Blood-Stained Robe
Isaiah 63:1–3 ("garments like his who treads in the winepress")
"He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God." (Revelation 19:13)
Treading the Winepress
Joel 3:13 & Isaiah 63:3 ("I trod them in my anger")
"He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty." (Revelation 19:15)
The Sharp Sword
Isaiah 11:4 ("strike the earth with the rod of his mouth")
"From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations..." (Revelation 19:15)

Tying the Entire Thread Back to "Dichotomy"
•The Winepress vs. The Cup of Communion: Notice the profound biblical contrast. At the Last Supper, Jesus took the fruit of the vine—crushed in the winepress of God's wrath on the cross—and offered it as the cup of the New Covenant for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:27–28). Those who reject His sacrifice must face the winepress themselves in Revelation 19.
•The Sword of Truth Completes the Cut: In Hebrews 4:12, the sharp two-edged sword divides soul and spirit internally for purification. In Revelation 19:15, that exact same sharp sword proceeds from the mouth of The Word of God to execute the final, external separation between His eternal Kingdom and all remaining rebellion.

Would you like to look at the geography mentioned in Isaiah 63:1 ("Edom" and "Bozrah") and how it connects to the "outside the city" location in Revelation 14:20, or explore how The Word of God as a sword ties Hebrews 4:12 and Revelation 19.15…..

U.S. Army Private First Class, Floyd K. Lindstrom of Holdrege, Nebraska, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor for his heroic actions on November 11, 1943, near Mignano, Italy.

Lindstrom joined the Army in June 1942 and was assigned to Company H, 2nd Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division. On November 11, 1943, Lindstrom was serving as a private first class, attempting to climb the treacherous slopes of Mount la Difensa while under heavy gunfire from German soldiers. On that day, near Mignano, Italy, he single-handedly charged and captured a German machine gun, killed a soldier and sent the others in the nest running for safety. He began shooting other soldiers and risked his life to get more ammunition.

He was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor for his actions on November 11, 1943.  On January 22, 1944, he landed at an Anzio beachhead with his unit, although he had been offered duty away from the fighting. On February 3, he was killed in a German counterattack. He was first listed as missing in action, and on June 6, 1944, his status was changed to killed in action. He is buried next to his mother in Evergreen Cemetery in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

and i told myself that dp just wanted to keep it forever or potentially wanted it to go to an exhibit or museum

i occasionally subtly joked on tweets that i was holding a spot for it within my collection of dp originals, but no sign or clue was given if it would ever be made available for purchase

i'm writing to help people understand dp

dp doesn't have a twitter gc, a telegram gc, or a cabal that he actively communicates with

he may not respond to dms and honestly the best way to interact with him is direct from his tweets

i've grown to respect this approach
it's not for everyone and probably can't be afforded to most artists trying to gain a loyal fan base

the guy just keeps his focus simple

he doubles down on what he does best
creating art

he supports the chains and people that allow for the vision of what these can offer the world
and he eliminates what he either is not interested in (being a customer service centric business &/or cabal community leader) or what does not align with what he is trying to achieve/pursue
he is at the purest form, goal driven

it's clear that ima fan of his craft
my wife used to think that due to my open and enthusiastic support, there might be a sort of inherent perk or preferential treatment with his creations
but after constant responses to her on my position
i think she starts to see it my way

i support dp because i absolutely love his artwork

i can't think of any artist in the world that produces the what his portfolio represents

i am inspired by his drive
he feeds my curiosity in the degen and ct culture
i align with his values
and i respect his fairness

he provides a level and fair playing field for all
and makes those that 'need' his art in their lives
to have work hard in order to have a shot of securing it,
but also with a touch of luck

i am not entitled to anything in life
if i choose to go above and beyond
if i choose to give, to be selfless, to be supportive
i will never expect anything in return

so being able to secure this physical means a lot to me
because i stay active, i stay connected
stay alert, stay alive, as they say in the army
stay alert, get the perk as they should say with dp artwork

but understanding dp is a piecemeal operation
he flows organically and sometimes sporadically

literally the very first lengthy composition of this thoughts was published in his twitter article just last week
before that, you had to read glimpses of his thoughts in tweets, follow his flow and art movement pivots daily

that's why i set a goal for myself
to become a subject matter expert in degen poet
understand the flow of how his artwork is generated
how it gets released to the public for consumption
understand his collections, his interests, his place in this space

i felt that if i could be a goto for fellow collectors i can fill that void of uncertainty and well needed organization and clarity

so i will leave you all with this

knowing what i know from daily monitoring and active participation in degen poet's onchain solana art activities

i know in my heart and in my justification
that degen poet is the 2026 solana breakpoint artist of the year

if you hear differently this Friday, that doesn't take away from that artist and their own past year achievements, respect deserved to them

but i know what degen poet did this past year
and i know there is no other artist that can compete with those metrics

text:
Night Prayer for November 11, 2026 ~~ St. Martin

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

O my God, I adore Thee and thank Thee for all the graces granted me this day. I offer Thee my sleep and all the moments of this night. I place myself and all my loved ones in Thy sacred side and under the mantle of Our Blessed Mother. Let Thy holy angels stand watch and keep us in peace.

Your Word calls us: “Without having any other weapon or defensive armor than the name of Jesus and the sign of the cross, I would throw myself willingly into the midst of the squadrons of a whole army.” (St. Martin)

Forgive any infidelities of this day, when I may have been indifferent to Thy inspirations. Restore in me a docile heart that no longer resists the goad of grace. Come, Holy Spirit, Light of the heart ~~ fill me with sorrow for lost graces and resolve to be faithful tomorrow. Grant me rest free from the sadness and bitterness that come from unfaithfulness as I rest in St. Martin. Amen.

Prayer inspired by Rev. M. Hamon, S.S., Meditations for All the Days of the Year, 3rd Edition, 1894.

text:
On the night of April 18, 1775, Dr. Joseph Warren was the most important Patriot leader still in Boston. When he learned British troops were heading for Lexington and Concord, he sent two riders out to warn the countryside. One of them was Paul Revere.

Warren was a physician, a fiery orator, and president of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress. On June 14, 1775, he was commissioned a major general. Three days later, the British attacked the American fortifications on Breed's Hill outside Boston.

Warren went anyway. When he arrived, the officers offered him command. He refused, saying he had come to fight, not to lead, and took a musket into the redoubt as a volunteer.

The Americans threw back two British assaults. On the third, they ran out of powder. As the British poured over the walls, Warren was among the last to leave the redoubt. He was shot in the head and killed instantly.

The British recognized him. His body was stripped, bayoneted, and thrown into a shallow grave with another dead American. One British officer later bragged that he'd stuffed the rebel into a hole.

Ten months later, after the British evacuated Boston in March 1776, Warren's brothers went to find him. By then the remains were unrecognizable. They brought someone who might be able to help.

Paul Revere was a silversmith, but he also did dental work on the side. A couple of years earlier, he had carved a replacement tooth from hippopotamus ivory and wired it into Warren's jaw. Digging through the grave, Revere found the jaw and recognized his own handiwork.

It is considered the first forensic dental identification in American history.

The man Warren had sent riding into history was the one who brought him home.

🔻 Sound Waves vs. Cancer: A Breakthrough in Immune Therapy! 

Imagine a future where cancer treatment is less about harsh chemicals and more about precise sound waves. Groundbreaking research from the University of Michigan is turning this vision into reality with a technique called histotripsy.

What is Histotripsy?
Histotripsy uses focused ultrasound waves to physically destroy tumors. But here’s the exciting part: it doesn’t just obliterate cancer cells; it also triggers a powerful immune response against the disease throughout the body!

How Does it Work?
Traditional treatments often destroy tumor antigens (proteins unique to cancer cells) along with the cancer. Histotripsy, however, breaks down the cancer cells’ protective walls, releasing these antigens intact. This exposure allows the body’s immune system to finally “see” and attack the cancer, even preventing its spread to other areas.

In mouse studies, this innovative approach led to the complete disappearance of tumors, even when only 50-75% of the mass was treated. More impressively, the immune response prevented recurrence and metastasis in over 80% of the animals. Researchers even found that injecting the debris from treated tumors into other mice provided a “vaccine-like” protection against cancer growth.

The Future of Cancer Treatment?
This non-invasive method offers a two-pronged attack: direct tumor destruction and immune system activation, all without the harmful side effects of radiation or chemotherapy. While human trials are ongoing, histotripsy holds immense promise for revolutionizing cancer care.

"Some California homeowners just got hit with a 350 dollar monthly increase on homes they already own.

Here’s how that happens. At Riviera Mobile Home Park in Encinitas, residents own their manufactured homes, but they lease the land underneath them. Starting November 1st, some of those space fees jump roughly 350 dollars a month, and some residents saw increases as high as 17 percent this year.

Most California apartment renters are protected by a statewide cap of up to 10 percent a year. Manufactured home owners leasing their space have no statewide cap at all. More than 100 California cities and counties have stepped in with their own limits. Oceanside caps increases at 8 percent. Encinitas doesn’t, so residents are asking the City Council for an emergency pause while the city considers a permanent cap.

And they can’t just leave. Moving a manufactured home costs a fortune. When they try to sell, buyers see a space fee with no ceiling, and the value of the home collapses. Residents say the park then offers to buy the homes back for next to nothing.

Agents, if you list or sell a manufactured home in a park, the space fee is the deal. Pull the rent history. Find out if that city or county caps increases. Put it in front of your buyer before they fall in love with the house.

The bigger lesson? These homeowners own the box and rent the land, and whoever owns the land makes the rules. A lot of agents run their business the same way. They own the hustle and rent the income, and every month it resets to zero. Own the dirt, in your home and in your business.

Do you think it’s right that so many California cities have no cap on manufactured home space rent? Tell me in the comments 👇

Shoutout to The Cool Down and Ray Brennan, plus CBS 8 San Diego, for some of the info in this reel 🙌
