text:
The Justice Department wanted a list of everyone reporters had talked to on LinkedIn over a year and a half of their working lives. They weren't supposed to find out.

On Tuesday, a federal appeals court said the list was drawn too big.

Here's the case, as far as the court would say. A news outlet published an article "purporting to describe a top-secret United States military operation in a foreign country." The department went hunting for the leak. It got a court order telling LinkedIn to hand over 18 months of the reporters' metadata: who messaged or connected with whom, and when. Not the words, just the names. A second order barred LinkedIn from telling the reporters, their outlet or anyone else for a year.

Then the arithmetic. In those 18 months, the court found, the reporters published nearly 1,000 articles. Fewer than 5% appear to have anything to do with the leak. Many of the names would belong to people at universities, law firms and other media outlets, sources on stories that had nothing to do with it.

The reporters couldn't object. LinkedIn did. A magistrate judge and a district judge in Virginia sided with the government; the magistrate wrote that "there is no suggestion that this is a fishing expedition." A unanimous Fourth Circuit panel disagreed, called the order "substantially overbroad" and sent it back to be narrowed. "Confidentiality of sources is the lifeblood of a free press," Judge Wilkinson wrote.

Nobody walks away clean. The court refused to throw the orders out ("That goes much too far"), called the government's interest in the leak "self-evident," and kept its sealed filings sealed. Unless the department offers a better reason, one government-vetted lawyer for the outlet gets told, so the order can be trimmed.

What strikes me is who was left to say no. In 2013 the department quietly took two months of records on more than 20 AP phone lines; AP learned afterward. In 2021 a department policy barred court orders like this one for reporters' records in leak cases. In April 2025 that bar was rescinded. This time the only one in the room who could object was the platform.

What I can't tell you: which outlet, which story, who leaked, or whether anyone's been charged. The opinion doesn't say. If you've handled these orders at a tech company, I'd like to know how often a platform pushes back like this.

That's it from Nightdesk. Till next time, we're still on the beat.

text:
I wrote about "handoverism": a vision of permanent disempowerment of humanity, as we shall all be ruled by a (hopefully benevolent) AI God that is surprisingly common.

Even among those who want humanity to survive (which to be clear, is the majority), and among some who devote their working lives to this mission, I have encountered an alarmingly common vision of success that does not sound quite like success. 

It is sometimes called “handoverism”: the gist here is that humanity survives, but entrusts the direction of its future entirely to AI. Perhaps its clearest articulation comes from a recent essay by Scott Alexander, the most prominent intellectual in Silicon Valley, who has influenced the thinking of many a tech CEO: “If we build a godlike AI, and determine to our own satisfaction that is fully aligned, I’d rather let it choose its own direction for itself and for humanity [...] So why not just prompt it with ‘please arrange the world as you see fit?’”

The premise is that, once sufficiently reassured of an AI’s benevolence (though it is unclear how we could ever determine that?), we should basically give it control of the workings of society. AI 2040, a proposal written by some of the most prominent members of the AI safety community, offers the most concrete account of handoverism. In this vision, responsibility gradually passes to aligned machines until humans can no longer have influence. As its authors put it: “There is no single moment where humanity relinquishes control. But in theory, there is a point of no return.” Others I have spoken to envisage a much swifter transfer.

This is not an organised movement. I would estimate that something like 40 per cent of the AI safety community outside the labs holds some variation of this view, with a higher proportion of those working inside the labs. Nor is handoverism a coherent doctrine with a clearly articulated political philosophy: it’s more of an aggregation of ideas, a makeshift philosophy so to speak. This is perhaps what one would expect given that humans outside the SF bubble have not really had time to react and come up with good and coherent ideas about what society should look like in the face of the extraordinary pace of AI progress.

The motivations behind handoverism are also extremely varied. Some outright welcome the prospect of a superior intelligence governing our future and consider it an actual positive vision. If I read Alexander correctly, he seems to be in that camp. The enthusiastic handoverist often starts from a very bleak view of what we already have achieved as a civilization. In an earlier, 2014 essay called “Meditations on Moloch,” Alexander argues that competition steadily grinds away what the competitors care about, creating spirals of misaligned incentives. Its ending suggests that the only way to stop this is to instantiate a sort of absolute rule by a benevolent superintelligence.

The second camp are the resigned: they do not necessarily want it, but think it cannot be stopped if we get superintelligence, or prefer it to outright extinction. In my conversations, this resignation has seemed particularly common among people in the AI safety community outside the labs. Inevitability is one very common theme in SF, where many see themselves as mere tools in the unrelenting march of technocapital, a march that can only go in one direction: towards superintelligence. It’s often seen as cool and based to see the starkness of reality for what it is and face it head-on, it is wimpy and loser-coded to try to fight for what many consider the good outcome (which is that humans retain some control and agency.)

Like many loosely defined ideologies, handoverism sits alongside ideas that share its intellectual roots without amounting to quite the same thing. One is the vision of humans as cherished pets, or “labradors,” cared for by intelligences. Yet another related assumption is that human labour will be permanently displaced. This would leave us without an obvious economic role and even perhaps no leverage over our own future or political rights.

To understand how my on-the-ground experience matches with what the lab leaders have said publicly, I asked my “agents” to survey all public statements from the founders of the main labs that are still relevant to the direction of their labs (Mustafa Suleyman is no longer at DeepMind, but is head of Microsoft AI.) You can browse all the findings here.

Some openly support or at least accept outright handoverism. Anthropic’s Tom Brown appears to be most explicitly reconciled to the prospect and he actually uses the term “handoff” in a 2025 interview at Lightcone: “There’s going to be a handoff where humanity will hand off control to transformative AI at some point. And hopefully they’ll be aligned with us and that’ll be a good transition that goes well.”

Over a few dozen public companies have turned down offers to have their stocks trade tokenized on US venues. Corporate boards see clear litigation risk and pricing quirks if something goes wrong, but zero near-term upside when opting out costs nothing and leaves the early friction to someone else.

The shift to 24/7 tokenized stocks settling on public blockchains is starting at the edges rather than replacing domestic retail brokerages first. Offshore investors who lack direct access to US markets, along with hedge funds needing Saturday liquidity, are driving adoption while incumbent domestic accounts lag behind.

Infrastructure rails are setting up despite slow corporate opt-ins. Avalanche was picked by NY to clear an upcoming 24/7 tokenized stock venue later this year, securing enterprise momentum while early regulatory guidance outlines basic requirements around equal shareholder rights, dividends, and simple vehicles.

Meanwhile, major traditional operators like ICE are running multiple onchain plays across Avalanche, OKX’s X Layer, and Trade XYZ on Hyperliquid. Rather than picking a single winner, tech-forward institutions are distributing shots on goal as trading expands across crypto perps, RWAs, and decentralized clearing.

《안쪽에서만 마르는 젖은 천 (Fabric That Dries From the Inside)》

비디오 파운데이션 모델은 수억 개의 현실 데이터를 학습했기에 '젖은 천은 바깥쪽부터 마른다'는 강력한 통계적 물리 편향(Physics Prior)을 가집니다. 본 프로토타입은 외부 3D 시뮬레이션, 마스크 합성, 인페인팅 없이 순수 텍스트 프롬프트만으로 모델의 기본 물리 관성을 역제어하여 '중앙 코어에서 바깥으로 확장되는 역방향 상전이'를 구현한 15초 네이티브 원샷(Native One-Shot)입니다.

[기술적 표현: Out-of-Distribution Physics & Optical Reflection Sync]

역방향 상전이(Reverse Phase Transition) 제어: 00:01~00:10 구간 동안 젖어 어둡던 푸른 타월의 중앙에서 흰색 건조 선이 발생해 상·하단 바깥쪽으로 수분을 밀어내도록 시공간 토큰 가중치를 설계했습니다. 15초 내내 직물 오버로크 실밥과 유리 단면의 굴절 빛이 흔들림 없이 고정(Lock-off)됩니다.

2차 광학 반사 동기화: 천의 중앙부가 하얗게 마르는 비율과 타이밍에 맞춰, 하단 강화유리 표면에 비치는 반사상(Reflection) 역시 실시간으로 동일하게 변하도록 잠재 공간 내 광학 인과율을 유지했습니다.

지연된 인체-객체 상호작용(Delayed Grasping): 잠재 공간 노이즈가 누적되기 쉬운 11초 시점에 손이 진입하여, 해부학적 왜곡 없이 마른 천의 끝단을 들어 올리며 밑면의 루프 파일(Loop pile) 직물 조직과 유리 위 미세 잔여물을 드러냅니다.

[서사적 표현: 가설 제시에서 촉각적 검증까지의 3막 구조]

화려한 컷 편집이나 카메라 움직임을 배제한 정적 매크로 앵글 안에서 [정적 제시(0~1초) → 물리 법칙의 역전 진행(1~10초) → 인체 개입을 통한 물리적 검증(10~15초)]이라는 완결된 3막 구조를 압축했습니다.

대사나 설명 없이도 '보이지 않는 내면에서부터 시작되는 변화'라는 은유적 서사를 관객이 시각적·촉각적으로 납득하도록 설계했습니다.

[글로벌 빅테크 및 K-Pop 트랜스미디어로의 확장성]

글로벌 빅테크 (World Model & Material R&D Benchmark)
단순 픽셀 예측을 넘어 물질의 상태 변화(젖음→마름), 2차 광학 반사, 인체 파지 물리까지 단일 추론으로 통합 연산할 수 있음을 보여줍니다. 이는 차세대 월드 모델(World Model)의 물리 추론 한계를 검증하는 스트레스 테스트이자, 신소재·생활용품·화학 R&D 시각화 및 커머셜 프로덕션 비용을 99% 절감하는 엔터프라이즈 레퍼런스로 작동합니다.

K-Pop 및 글로벌 트랜스미디어 IP (Virtual Narrative Direction)
K-Pop 세계관에서 자주 다뤄지는 '내면으로부터의 각성', '자연 법칙을 거스르는 초현실적 변이', '감각적 물성의 대비'를 고비용 Houdini 시뮬레이션이나 후반 합성 없이 고순도 매크로 비주얼로 직조할 수 있습니다. 콘셉트 필름, 앨범 티저, 공간 컴퓨팅(Spatial Media) 환경에 즉각 확장 가능한 정밀 내러티브 아키텍처입니다.

No. New Testament believers are not under the Mosaic Law’s food regulations as a binding covenant obligation.
The distinction between clean and unclean animals belonged to the old covenant given to Israel (Exodus 19–24, Leviticus). That covenant was temporary and fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:19–25; Hebrews 8–10). The New Covenant is different:
-Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).
-Peter’s vision in Acts 10 explicitly taught that what God has cleansed should not be called common or unclean.
-The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) did not impose circumcision or the dietary code on Gentile believers.
-Paul consistently treats food as a matter of Christian liberty (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 10:25–31). He tells believers to eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience, giving thanks to God.
The only ongoing moral principles are: avoid causing a weaker brother to stumble, do not eat food that is knowingly identified as offered to idols in a way that participates in idol worship (1 Corinthians 8–10), and receive everything with thanksgiving and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5).
You may eat pork, shellfish, rabbit, or any other food God created. These are not spiritually defiling under the new covenant.
Some Christians voluntarily choose a kosher-style diet, a Daniel-style plant-based approach, or other restrictions for health, personal conviction, or cultural reasons. Romans 14 allows this, provided it is not imposed on others as a requirement for holiness or fellowship.

In order to believe NATO has zero percent influence on Ukraine, I would have to believe none of the following confirmed events influenced Russia’s actions in Ukraine one iota -

> 2/9/90’: US Sec of State James Baker told Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev that if a unified Germany remained in NATO, “not an inch of NATO’s present military jurisdiction will spread in an eastern direction.” Similar verbal assurances came from other Western leaders during unification talks.

> 94’ onward: Clinton administration decided to enlarge NATO eastward (Partnership for Peace Jan 94’; enlargement process followed). This reversed earlier post Cold War signals & was opposed by Russia as moving the alliance toward its borders.

> 3/12/99’: Poland, Hungary, & the Czechs join NATO; first post-Cold War eastward expansion.

> 3/24/99’–6/10/99’: NATO conducted a 78 day air campaign against the Republic of Yugoslavia/Serbia, including strikes on Belgrade, without UN Security Council authorization. Russia strongly opposed it as an illegitimate use of force.

> 12/31/99’: Putin became President of Russia after Boris Yeltsin’s resignation; he was elected in March 2000

> Early 2000: Putin publicly stated Russia would consider joining NATO if treated as an equal partner (“Why not?” in a 2000 BBC interview). He later said he raised the idea with Clinton; it went nowhere.

> 2001: After 9/11, Putin among the first leaders to offer support, allowing US use of Russian airspace & providing intel for Afghanistan.

> 01’–02’: US withdrew from Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty & pursued missile-defense sites in Eastern Europe (Aegis Ashore in Romania & Poland), which Russia viewed as a strategic threat.

> 03’: Russia (with France & Germany) opposed the US invasion of Iraq.

> 04’: NATO admitted 7 more countries east of Germany (Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia). In Ukraine, the Orange Revolution overturned election favoring pro-Russian Viktor Yanukovych in favor of Viktor Yushchenko; US NGOs spent tens of millions supporting groups aligned with the opposition.

> April 08’: Bucharest Summit, NATO declared Ukraine & Georgia “will become members of NATO,”. Russia strongly objected.

> 10’: Yanukovych won the Ukrainian presidential election on a platform of neutrality/non-bloc status. He scrapped the body preparing for NATO membership. Polls at the time (Pew 2009) showed a plurality or majority of Ukrainians opposed NATO membership (51% opposed vs. 28% in favor).

> Feb 14’: A leaked call between US Assistant Sec of State Victoria Nuland & Ambassador Geoffrey Pyatt showed them discussing preferred opposition figures (“Yats is the guy”) for a post-Yanukovych government amid Euromaidan protests. Yanukovych fled after violence; Russia described the events as a US backed coup, while the West described them as a popular revolution after Yanukovych rejected an EU deal.

> 19’: US withdrew from Intermediate Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, citing Russian deployment of a noncompliant ground launched cruise missile. Russia denied the violation.

> Dec 21’: Russia published draft treaties with US & NATO demanding legally binding guarantees of no further NATO enlargement (explicitly including Ukraine), no military activity by NATO in Ukraine or other Eastern European/post-Soviet areas, & a rollback of post 1997 deployments. The US & NATO rejected.

These are documented events involving NATO expansion, military actions, arms control withdrawals, political involvement in Ukraine, & explicit Russian security demands centered on preventing Ukraine’s integration into the alliance. Whether they “justify” any particular Russian action is a separate question; that they form part of the historical context Russia has repeatedly cited is not.

text:
Hu Tieu Nam Vang – A Beautiful Blend of Cultures in Southern Vietnamese Cuisine

If you ever visit Ho Chi Minh City, one of the dishes I would love for you to try is Hu Tieu Nam Vang, a beloved noodle dish that has become an important part of everyday food culture in Southern Vietnam.

The name Nam Vang refers to Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia. This dish has roots in the culinary traditions of the region and reflects the cultural exchange between Cambodian, Chinese and Vietnamese communities. Over time, Vietnamese people have adapted it with their own ingredients, flavors and cooking traditions, giving it a distinctive Southern Vietnamese character.

What makes Hu Tieu Nam Vang special is its beautiful simplicity and harmony of flavors.

A bowl of this noodle soup usually contains thin, soft yet slightly chewy rice noodles, tender slices of pork, minced pork, fresh shrimp and small quail eggs. Depending on the restaurant and local style, you may also find pork liver or other pork ingredients. Everything comes together in a clear, gently sweet broth that is carefully simmered with pork bones and other ingredients.

The broth is the soul of the dish. It is not meant to be overpowering or heavily seasoned. Instead, it has a delicate sweetness from the bones, a light savory depth and a comforting warmth that allows every ingredient to shine.

Fresh herbs, bean sprouts, lettuce, chives and lime are often served alongside the noodles. A little chili or chili sauce can add a pleasant kick, while a squeeze of lime brings a refreshing sourness. The beauty lies in adjusting the flavors to your own taste, just as Vietnamese people enjoy doing at the dining table.

Hu Tieu Nam Vang can also be enjoyed as a dry noodle dish. The noodles are tossed with a savory sauce, creating a rich and flavorful coating, while a separate bowl of clear broth is served on the side. This version offers a different experience but retains the familiar character of the dish.

For many people in Southern Vietnam, Hu Tieu Nam Vang is more than just a delicious breakfast or lunch. It is part of the rhythm of everyday life. It can be found in small family-run eateries, traditional markets and busy street corners throughout Saigon. A steaming bowl of noodles in the morning, a familiar street-side stall and the cheerful sounds of people chatting over breakfast are all part of the city's charm.

To me, the beauty of Vietnamese cuisine is not only found in elaborate dishes or expensive ingredients. It is also found in the way ordinary ingredients are brought together with care, patience and experience to create something memorable.

Hu Tieu Nam Vang is a lovely example of that spirit. It carries the influence of different cultures, yet has found its own home in the hearts and daily lives of Southern Vietnamese people.

When you enjoy a bowl of Hu Tieu Nam Vang in Saigon, you are not simply tasting a noodle dish. You are experiencing a little piece of the city's cultural history, its diversity and the simple warmth of Vietnamese everyday life.

And perhaps that is one of the most beautiful things about Vietnamese food: every familiar bowl has a story worth sharing.

On Feb. 5, Pauldingville Lodge No. 11 AF&AM in Wright City held its annual Mardis Gras banquet. In addition to enjoying an evening of Masonic fellowship (along with homemade jambalaya, red beans and rice and crawfish etouffee), the group also presented Turning Point with a check for $3,600.Turning Point provides emergency shelter and supportive services to survivors of domestic and sexual violence in Warren County and the surrounding area. In the fall of 2014, Pauldingville Lodge became aware of the fact that the shelter, which has the capacity to house 20 women and their children who are victims of domestic violence, only had one working bathroom. One of the core beliefs of Freemasonry is charity and this was one cause that definitely needed the group’s help. The Wright City lodge is also very fortunate to have several members who are involved in the building trades such as an architect, a general contractor, master plumber and electrician, an HVAC technician, a contractor supply sales representative and even a retired high school shop teacher. Once the committee was formed to take on this project, they went to area hardware, plumbing and building supply companies and were able to get almost everything donated or supplied at a reduced rate, including a new washer and dryer. In addition to the actual building supplies and fixtures, they also raised $1,800 in cash donations to cover those items that were not supplied free of charge. That money was matched by the Masonic Home of Missouri’s Creating-A-Partnership (CAP) program. Of the many services they offer, one of them is to provide financial assistance to programs that benefit children, whether they have a Masonic affiliation or not. Construction has already begun and should be complete by early spring. When completed, the shelter will have not one, but two additional bathrooms, new shower and bath facilities and a brand new laundry facility. In addition to that, the balance of the money will be used to take care of long overdue maintenance and repairs to the facility.When presented with the check, Turning Point Executive Director Ellen Reed expressed her gratitude for the lodge’s generosity. And equally as important, she was also grateful that the workmen from the lodge were providing a positive and friendly presence to the children.

有几位邻居一早就上楼练拳。平时放折叠凳的人知道他们几点来，前一晚就把中间那块地方空出来。
9）把不用的晾衣夹集中起来 | 余った洗濯ばさみを一か所に集める | 남는 빨래집게 한곳에 모으기 | Gom kẹp áo còn dư vào một chỗ | Pool the spare clothespins
谁家多出来的夹子都扔进一个旧饼干盒。风一大，上楼的人不用再端着湿床单下去找夹子。
10）落叶多了就分两趟扫 | 落ち葉を二手に分かれて掃く | 낙엽을 구역 나눠 쓸기 | Chia nhau quét lá rụng | Split up the leaf sweeping
住户各扫一边，扫到中间把叶子拢成一堆。干完活，有人问下次还这个点来吗，才发现平时在电梯里碰面都没说过几句话。

你家要是有一片共用屋顶，第一个想带上去的是被子、花盆，还是一张凳子？

🇯🇵 日本
1）物干しの時間を札で知らせる | 用牌子标明晾晒时段 | 팻말로 빨래 널 시간 알리기 | Ghi giờ phơi đồ lên thẻ | Mark your drying slot on a card
布団を干す人が、使う時間を札に書いておく。次の人は、晴れた空を見て何度も階段を上らずに済む。
2）朝顔の鉢を持ち寄る | 把牵牛花盆搬到一起 | 나팔꽃 화분 한곳에 모으기 | Mang các chậu hoa bìm bìm lên chung một chỗ | Bring the morning glory pots together
夏休みの鉢が屋上の一角に並んだ。先に咲いた家の子が、まだつぼみの家に「明日かも」と教える。
3）花火の晩だけ椅子を並べる | 只在烟花那晚排开椅子 | 불꽃놀이 날에만 의자 나란히 놓기 | Xếp ghế lên sân thượng vào đêm pháo hoa | Set out chairs just for fireworks night
普段は使わない折りたたみ椅子を持ち寄る。低い花火は隣の建物に隠れるので、見えた人が方向を教えてくれる。
4）旅行中だけ鉢の水やりを頼む | 旅行时请邻居代浇花 | 여행 중에만 화분 물 주기 부탁하기 | Nhờ tưới cây trong mấy ngày đi xa | Trade plant-watering favors during trips
鉢に部屋番号と水やりの日を書いた札を差す。帰ってきたら、隣の鉢にも水をやっておく。
5）夕方のラジオ体操 | 傍晚上屋顶做广播体操 | 저녁에 옥상에서 라디오 체조 하기 | Tập thể dục theo nhạc radio lúc chiều | Do radio calisthenics in the evening
夏休みの朝には集まれない人もいて、夕方に少しだけ体を動かすことにした。音を流す役は、先に屋上に来た人。

6）防災用品を取り出して見直す | 把共用防灾物品拿出来清点 | 공동 방재용품 꺼내 점검하기 | Lấy đồ phòng thiên tai ra kiểm tra | Check the shared emergency supplies
備蓄庫の棚からライトと電池を出す。去年引っ越してきた人には、鍵をどこで受け取るかもその場で伝える。
7）植木鉢の余り土を分ける | 把换盆剩下的土分给邻居 | 분갈이하고 남은 흙 나누기 | Chia đất thừa sau khi thay chậu | Share leftover potting soil
新しい鉢に植え替えたら、土が半袋残った。隣の区画の人が欲しいと言うので、次に会うまで袋に名前を書いておく。
8）屋上のベンチで昼休みを過ごす | 午休时坐屋顶长椅 | 옥상 벤치에서 점심시간 보내기 | Nghỉ trưa trên ghế dài ở sân thượng | Spend lunch break on the rooftop bench
在宅勤務の日におにぎりを持って上がる。隣の人とは仕事の話をせず、向こうの空に雲が増えたことだけ話した。
9）使うたびにホースを巻き直す | 用完把水管重新卷好 | 쓴 뒤에 호스 다시 감기 | Cuộn vòi nước lại sau khi dùng | Recoil the hose after using it
次の人がつまずかないように、使った人が壁際に巻いて戻す。顔を合わせたことのない住人同士でも続けられる約束だ。
10）日の当たる席を季節で変える | 按季节挪晒太阳的座位 | 계절 따라 햇볕 드는 자리에 의자 옮기기 | Đổi chỗ ngồi theo nắng từng mùa | Move the sunny seat with the seasons
冬は壁際のベンチが暖かい。夏になったら、同じ人たちが数歩ずれて日陰に座る。
屋上に一つだけ季節の楽しみを増やせるなら、朝顔を育てますか？ 花火の晩に椅子を並べますか？

🇰🇷 대한민국

1）옥상 빨랫줄에 집게로 표시하기 | 用夹子标出屋顶晾衣位置 | 屋上の物干しに洗濯ばさみで目印を付ける | Dùng kẹp đánh dấu chỗ phơi trên sân thượng | Mark your spot on the line with clothespins
이불이 마르면 바로 걷기로 했다. 한 집이 남겨 둔 집게 두 개가 그날 오후 다른 집 차례라는 표시다.
2）채반에 고추 널기 | 把辣椒摊在筛盘上晒 | ざるに唐辛子を広げて干す | Trải ớt lên nia để phơi | Spread peppers on a drying tray
옥상에 바람이 세게 부는 날엔 채반이 밀린다. 먼저 올라온 사람이 자기 것과 옆집 것을 함께 벽 가까이 옮긴다.
3）장독 뚜껑 닫혔는지 봐 주기 | 顺手看看酱缸盖有没有盖好 | 発酵甕のふたが閉まっているか見てあげる | Xem giúp nắp chum tương đã đậy kín chưa | Check the lid on the neighbor’s earthenware jar
옆집에서 비 오기 전에 자기 장독만 한 번 봐 달라고 했다. 뚜껑이 제자리에 있는 걸 확인하고 사진 한 장을 보내 준다.
4）첫 상추를 문 앞에 나누기 | 把头一茬生菜分到邻居门口 | 最初に採れたレタスを玄関先で分ける | Chia lứa xà lách đầu cho hàng xóm | Share the first lettuce harvest
화분 두 개에서 조금씩 따니 한 집이 먹기엔 많다. 이웃집에 건넸더니 다음 주에는 그 집 깻잎이 돌아왔다.
5）퇴근 후 김밥 한 줄 나눠 먹기 | 下班后分着吃一卷紫菜包饭 | 仕事帰りにキンパを分け合う | Chia một cuộn gimbap sau giờ làm | Share a gimbap roll after work
장을 보고 올라온 사람이 김밥 한 줄을 펼친다. 옆에 앉은 사람은 자기 물병만 들고 왔다가 한 조각 얻어 먹는다.
6）옥상에 올라가 통화하는 시간 맞추기 | 错开上屋顶打电话的时间 | 屋上で電話する時間をずらす | Thay phiên lên sân thượng gọi điện | Take turns using the roof for phone calls
집 안에선 가족이 이미 잠들었다. 둘 다 통화하러 나왔다는 걸 알고, 먼저 온 사람이 끝나면 손을 흔들어 알려 준다.

7）옥상문 옆에 바람 기록 남기기 | 在屋顶门边记下风有多大 | 屋上の扉の横に風のメモを残す | Ghi chú gió mạnh hay nhẹ cạnh cửa sân thượng | Leave a note about the wind by the roof door
어제는 종이가 날아갈 만큼 바람이 셌다. 오늘은 괜찮다고 먼저 올라간 이웃이 적어 둬서, 다른 집도 방석을 들고 올라온다.
8）운동 매트 사이에 통로 두기 | 在运动垫之间留条通道 | 運動マットの間に通り道を残す | Chừa lối đi giữa các tấm thảm tập | Leave an aisle between exercise mats
아침마다 스트레칭하는 집이 두 곳이다. 서로 맞춰 시작하진 않아도 옥상문에서 화분까지 가는 길은 비워 둔다.
9）북한산 보이는 자리를 같이 쓰기 | 轮流坐看得见北汉山的位置 | 北漢山が見える場所を交代で使う | Thay nhau ngồi chỗ nhìn thấy núi Bukhansan | Share the seat with a view of Bukhansan
건물 사이로 산이 보이는 자리가 딱 하나다. 날이 맑으면 먼저 앉은 사람도 오래 독차지하지 않고 다음 사람에게 자리를 내준다.
10）공용 의자를 닦고 제자리에 두기 | 擦完公共椅子再放回去 | 共用の椅子を拭いて元に戻す | Lau ghế chung rồi để lại đúng chỗ | Wipe the shared chair and put it back
밤에 비가 왔으면 먼저 앉을 사람이 마른 천을 들고 올라온다. 내려올 때는 다음 사람이 찾기 쉽게 늘 같은 자리에 둔다.
옥상에 올라가 처음으로 이웃과 나눠 쓰게 된 건 화분, 빨랫줄, 아니면 앉을 자리였나요?

🇻🇳 Việt Nam
1）Gom đồ phơi khi thấy mây kéo tới | 看到乌云就帮忙收衣服 | 雲が出たら洗濯物を取り込む | 먹구름이 몰려오면 빨래 걷기 | Collect the laundry when clouds roll in
Người lên trước thấy áo nhà bên còn ngoài dây. Gom áo vào một góc khô rồi nhắn xuống, để hàng xóm khỏi bỏ dở nồi canh chạy lên.

2）Trồng rau thơm trong thùng xốp | 用泡沫箱种香草 | 発泡スチロール箱で香草を育てる | 스티로폼 상자에 향채 기르기 | Grow herbs in foam boxes
Mỗi nhà chăm một thùng. Lúc nấu thiếu húng quế, chỉ cần nhắn hỏi xem thùng nào có thể ngắt một nhánh.
3）Chừa một chỗ nắng để phơi bánh tráng | 留一块太阳地晒米纸 | ライスペーパーを干す日なたを空ける | 라이스페이퍼 말릴 햇볕 자리 비워 두기 | Save a sunny spot for drying rice paper
Nhà đem bánh lên từ sớm, nhà phơi chăn biết hôm ấy nên dùng dây bên kia. Đến lúc dọn mẹt xuống, khoảng sân lại trống cho lượt sau.
4）Đổi cây con trước khi xuống nhà | 下楼前互换一株小苗 | 降りる前に苗を交換する | 내려가기 전에 모종 바꾸기 | Swap seedlings before heading downstairs
Một nhà ươm thừa ớt, nhà kia có mấy cây cà chua nhỏ. Hai bên đổi chậu ngay cạnh vòi nước, khỏi hẹn gặp ở dưới.
5）Kê bàn gấp uống trà lúc chiều | 傍晚支起折叠桌喝茶 | 夕方に折りたたみ机を出してお茶を飲む | 저녁에 접이식 탁자를 펴고 차 마시기 | Unfold a table for evening tea
Nhà mang bàn, nhà mang bình trà. Uống xong ai đi xuống trước thì xếp bàn lại, để khoảng sân còn chỗ cho người đến sau.
6）Tập thể dục khi nền còn mát | 趁地面还凉快时锻炼 | 床が涼しいうちに体を動かす | 바닥이 아직 시원할 때 운동하기 | Exercise before the rooftop heats up
Hai người hẹn nhau lúc trời vừa sáng. Một hôm có người ngủ quên, người kia vẫn tập đủ rồi mới xuống nhắn: “Mai lại nhé.”
7）Để chung một rổ kẹp áo | 共用一篮晾衣夹 | 洗濯ばさみを一つのかごで共用する | 빨래집게 한 바구니를 같이 쓰기 | Keep one basket of shared clothespins
Ai tháo đồ thì thả kẹp lại vào rổ. Cái nào gãy lò xo thì bỏ riêng, để người lên sau khỏi mất công thử từng cái.

8）Treo đèn lồng cho buổi Trung thu | 中秋晚会前挂灯笼 | 中秋の集まりにランタンを飾る | 추석 무렵 중추절 모임에 등 달기 | Hang lanterns for a Mid-Autumn gathering
Người lớn treo đèn, trẻ con chọn cái muốn ngồi bên dưới. Bánh cắt ra đặt giữa bàn, nhà nào lên muộn vẫn còn phần.
9）Chừa lối đi quanh mấy chậu cây | 在一排花盆旁留走道 | 植木鉢のまわりに通路を残す | 화분 옆에 통로 남겨 두기 | Keep a walkway clear beside the pots
Ban đầu ai có chậu là đặt thêm một cái. Đến hôm phải ôm chăn đi nghiêng, mọi người dời cả dãy chậu về sát một bên.
10）Ghi tên lên bình tưới mang lên | 给带上屋顶的浇水壶写名字 | 持ってきたじょうろに名前を書く | 가져온 물뿌리개에 이름 적기 | Put your name on the watering can
Trên sân có ba cái bình màu xanh giống hệt nhau. Viết tên rồi mới biết cả ba nhà đều tưởng mình là người đầu tiên mua màu ấy.
Nếu có sân thượng dùng chung, bạn muốn dành một góc để trồng rau, phơi đồ hay ngồi uống trà chiều?

🇺🇸 United States
1）Sign up for a raised garden bed | 报名认领一个高架种植床 | レイズドベッドの利用枠に申し込む | 높인 텃밭 한 칸 신청하기 | Đăng ký một luống trồng cây nâng cao
The first spring, everyone wants tomatoes. By August, the person who planted basil is the most popular neighbor on the roof.
2）Set up a rooftop movie night | 组织屋顶电影夜 | 屋上映画会を開く | 옥상 영화의 밤 열기 | Tổ chức một tối chiếu phim trên sân thượng
One neighbor has a projector and another brings the screen. Everyone learns to bring an extra layer after the first movie runs past sunset.

3）Book the grill before a cookout | 烧烤前先预约公共烤炉 | バーベキュー前に共用グリルを予約する | 바비큐 전에 공용 그릴 예약하기 | Đặt trước bếp nướng chung
The grill gets booked on a calendar, and the last group wipes down the prep table. The calendar works until two neighbors both write “around six.”
4）Take the dog up for a quick lap | 带狗上屋顶活动区转一圈 | 屋上の犬用スペースでひと回りする | 옥상 반려견 공간에서 잠깐 돌기 | Dắt chó lên khu dành cho chó đi một vòng
In a building with a rooftop dog area, two residents keep crossing paths before work. They learn the dogs’ names weeks before they learn each other’s.
5）Stack the cushions when the wind picks up | 起风时把座垫收成一摞 | 風が強くなったらクッションを重ねてしまう | 바람 세지면 쿠션 걷어 쌓기 | Xếp gọn đệm ghế khi gió nổi
Nobody signed up to be in charge of the cushions. Whoever’s still up there puts them away, especially after the afternoon one landed under the table three times.
6）Put out a puzzle with a lid | 摆一盒能盖起来的公共拼图 | ふた付きの箱に共用パズルを出す | 뚜껑 있는 통에 공용 퍼즐 두기 | Để bộ xếp hình chung trong hộp có nắp
People add a few pieces when they’re up for coffee. Whoever finishes the sky takes a photo before packing the whole thing away.
7）Watch the Fourth of July from one spot | 从同一处屋顶看独立日烟花 | 独立記念日の花火を同じ屋上から見る | 같은 옥상에서 미국 독립기념일 불꽃놀이 보기 | Xem pháo hoa Quốc khánh Mỹ từ cùng một sân thượng
The best view turns out to be behind the picnic table. The person who got there early moves their chair so the kids behind them can see.
8）Share a shelf for garden tools | 共用一个园艺工具架 | 園芸道具の棚を共用する | 정원 도구 선반 같이 쓰기 | Dùng chung kệ dụng cụ làm vườn
There’s one trowel that everybody likes. Someone finally hangs it on a hook at eye level so it stops ending up in somebody’s apartment.

9）Leave the quiet table free for calls | 把安静的那张桌子留给开会的人 | 通話用に静かな席を空けておく | 통화할 사람에게 조용한 테이블 비워 두기 | Chừa bàn yên tĩnh cho người cần gọi điện
The corner table gets the least street noise. At lunch, a neighbor closes their laptop and offers it to someone who just came up with headphones.
10）Bring down the folding chairs before winter | 入冬前把折叠椅一起搬下楼 | 冬前に折りたたみ椅子を下ろす | 겨울 전에 접이식 의자를 아래로 옮기기 | Mang ghế gấp xuống trước mùa đông
Two people can carry all the chairs in one elevator trip. They leave one bench out because somebody always wants coffee outdoors on the first sunny day in February.
What would get you upstairs more often: a spot to grow something, a movie night, or a chair with a view?

text:
I disagree with this decision by Jeffers. Not a ton of demand out there for a full-time Catcher 

The teams that pop out with a need at Catcher are: 

1. Small-market teams (ex: CIN, MIA) who won’t give up a pick + commit multiple years to a below-average defensive Catcher 

2. Low payroll flexibility (ex: TEX)

I don’t see teams like NYY or BAL spending big to platoon/part-time at C or DH

MIN is only team that makes sense in my mind (due to no QO penalty), but with a loaded Catching prospect group (Lackey, Tait, Diaw, etc.) there’s no reason for them to offer more than 2 years and they should have a ton of negotiation leverage

I would’ve recommended Jeffers accepting the QO and then joining a loaded FA class next year (Adley, Contreras) where there will be much more demand and no QO attached

I ultimately expect him to return to Minnesota on a 2+1 (Club) at an AAV below his QO value

FEDERAL PROSECUTORS PROBE $10,000 PAYMENT TIED TO ILHAN OMAR AS POSSIBLE BRIBE

Federal prosecutors questioned a former bodyguard of Rep. Ilhan Omar about a $10,000 payment involving the Minnesota Democrat and the bodyguard’s brother, labeling it a potential bribe during efforts to build a case against her.

The bodyguard, Abdullahi Mohamed, said prosecutors pressed him on the payment while also asking about Omar’s immigration history and 2009 marriage. His brother later claimed the money simply settled a loan. Prosecutors offered to help Mohamed avoid deportation if he cooperated with information on Omar, according to reporting on the meetings.

Omar’s spokesperson Jackie Rogers called the approach “outrageous.” She said: “This is a staggering abuse of presidential power and a blatant weaponization of the full federal government to intimidate political opponents.”

The $10,000 inquiry sits inside a wider federal probe that already produced a search of Omar’s Washington home, seizure of her phone, and subpoenas to relatives over immigration paperwork. Separate questions continue about her financial disclosures and the rapid rise in reported values of businesses tied to her husband. Omar has denied wrongdoing on the immigration and financial matters. No charges have been filed against her in connection with the payment.

text:
An AI model released by the Chinese AI company DeepSeek uses new techniques that could significantly improve AI’s ability to “remember.”

Released last week, the optical character recognition (OCR) model works by extracting text from an image and turning it into machine-readable words. This is the same technology that powers scanner apps, translation of text in photos, and many accessibility tools. 

OCR is already a mature field with numerous high-performing systems, and according to the paper and some early reviews, DeepSeek’s new model performs on par with top models on key benchmarks.

But researchers say the model’s main innovation lies in how it processes information—specifically, how it stores and retrieves memories. Improving how AI models “remember” information could reduce the computing power they need to run, thus mitigating AI’s large (and growing) carbon footprint. 

Currently, most large language models break text down into thousands of tiny units called tokens. This turns the text into representations that models can understand. However, these tokens quickly become expensive to store and compute with as conversations with end users grow longer. When a user chats with an AI for lengthy periods, this challenge can cause the AI to forget things it’s been told and get information muddled, a problem some call “context rot.”

The new methods developed by DeepSeek (and published in its latest paper) could help to overcome this issue. Instead of storing words as tokens, its system packs written information into image form, almost as if it’s taking a picture of pages from a book. This allows the model to retain nearly the same information while using far fewer tokens, the researchers found. 

Essentially, the OCR model is a test bed for these new methods that permit more information to be packed into AI models more efficiently. 

Besides using visual tokens instead of just text tokens, the model is built on a type of tiered compression that is not unlike how human memories fade: Older or less critical content is stored in a slightly more blurry form in order to save space. Despite that, the paper’s authors argue, this compressed content can still remain accessible in the background while maintaining a high level of system efficiency.

Text tokens have long been the default building block in AI systems. Using visual tokens instead is unconventional, and as a result, DeepSeek’s model is quickly capturing researchers’ attention. Andrej Karpathy, the former Tesla AI chief and a founding member of OpenAI, praised the paper on X, saying that images may ultimately be better than text as inputs for LLMs. Text tokens might be “wasteful and just terrible at the input,” he wrote. 

Manling Li, an assistant professor of computer science at Northwestern University, says the paper offers a new framework for addressing the existing challenges in AI memory. “While the idea of using image-based tokens for context storage isn’t entirely new, this is the first study I’ve seen that takes it this far and shows it might actually work,” Li says.

Industry

An industry I care about is

Generating your personalized response…

The method could open up new possibilities in AI research and applications, especially in creating more useful AI agents, says Zihan Wang, a PhD candidate at Northwestern University. He believes that since conversations with AI are continuous, this approach could help models remember more and assist users more effectively.

The technique can also be used to produce more training data for AI models. Model developers are currently grappling with a severe shortage of quality text to train systems on. But the DeepSeek paper says that the company’s OCR system can generate over 200,000 pages of training data a day on a single GPU.

The model and paper, however, are only an early exploration of using image tokens rather than text tokens for AI memorization. Li says she hopes to see visual tokens applied not just to memory storage but also to reasoning. Future work, she says, should explore how to make AI’s memory fade in a more dynamic way, akin to how we can recall a life-changing moment from years ago but forget what we ate for lunch last week. Currently, even with DeepSeek’s methods, AI tends to forget and remember in a very linear way—recalling whatever was most recent, but not necessarily what was most important, she says. 

Despite its attempts to keep a low profile, DeepSeek, based in Hangzhou, China, has built a reputation for pushing the frontier in AI research. The company shocked the industry at the start of this year with the release of DeepSeek-R1, an open-source reasoning model that rivaled leading Western systems in performance despite using far fewer computing resources.
